five_things: A Renfe high-speed train rammed the back of a stationary Iryo train south of Madrid, killing at least 68 people, after Spain's control centre reportedly told trains to resume moving following a signalling failure, a decision the transport minister called "inexplicable".
Israel's election is unresolved: with roughly 85 percent counted, Netanyahu's bloc has 53 seats and Eisenkot's 48, neither near the 61 needed, and both men say they will form a government.

Iran says it is in close contact with mediators on a seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while Trump denies ordering peace talks and says contact was about medical supplies, a distinction with remarkably little difference.
The Federal Reserve held rates at 3.75% to 4% on a 10-2 vote, with Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissenting in favour of a hike, so the only disagreement was over how much to worry about inflation.

Alphabet fell more than 10% after missing earnings estimates and posting negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion, while Oracle rose 11% on a promise of $225 billion in revenue in fiscal 2030, proving that investors reward ambition only when it arrives on a slide.

articles.headline: Israel Votes, Counts, and Discovers Nobody Has 61 of the 120 Seats
articles.dek: With about 85 to 90 percent of ballots counted, Netanyahu's bloc leads with 53 seats to Eisenkot's 48, and 19 Arab-party seats hold the arithmetic.
articles.catch_up: Israel held its first general election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faced former military chief Gadi Eisenkot in a vote widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership.
articles.why_it_matters: Weeks of coalition bargaining, and possibly another election, will decide who runs a country at war and what happens to its judiciary, its military draft rules and its relations abroad. Israeli politics is again in the hands of the arithmetic, not the voters' stated preferences.
body: Partial results show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel's election without a majority. With about 85 percent of ballots counted, the BBC reported, Likud and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies were on track for 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties were set for 48. A majority requires 61, a number neither side is near, which is the sort of detail that tends to matter in elections.

Both men have said they will form a government. Translation: both men intend to be asked, and both have told the public that the public has already asked. Netanyahu declared a "great majority" at Likud headquarters. Eisenkot said the public had "spoken in favour of change." The two claims cannot both be right, though the count suggests they can both be wrong.

The exit polls did not help. Three broadcasters first projected 52 or 53 seats for Eisenkot's bloc against 50 for Netanyahu's. Updated versions had two showing a 51-51 tie and one giving Netanyahu a three-seat lead. As counting went on, Netanyahu's bloc outperformed the polls at 53, though the BBC noted that is still 15 seats fewer than it once controlled in the last Knesset.

The real story is the 19 seats projected for Arab-led parties, the United Arab List and the Joint List, an unprecedented figure that nearly doubles their representation. The BBC attributed this to a surge in turnout among Arab Israelis, who are about a fifth of the population. In theory, that makes them kingmakers. In practice, all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them, so the kingmakers have been invited to the coronation on the condition that they not attend.

Netanyahu has warned against a government relying on "anti-Zionist Arab parties." Eisenkot has previously attached conditions to such cooperation, including recognition of Israel as Jewish and democratic, and the right-wing parties in his own bloc have flatly rejected it. Al Jazeera reported that Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said the alliance could back an anti-Netanyahu government from outside but would not join it. He also said the opposition "cannot dictate any conditions." That is a hard negotiating position for a party the other side says it will not negotiate with.

Likud, meanwhile, said the election was "stolen," alleging bribery, threats, violence, fraud and prohibited software, which Al Jazeera's account directs at Arab parties. The BBC noted the claims came without evidence, and the Central Elections Committee said it would examine them in a post-election review. Likud said it was passing hundreds of testimonies to the police, the Shin Bet and the committee. This is a notable position for a bloc that leads the count.

What happens next is procedural. Between roughly 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots, from soldiers, diplomats and hospital patients, remain uncounted (Al Jazeera put it above 500,000), so seat totals could still move. After official results, President Isaac Herzog will consult every faction and invite the leader he thinks has the best chance to try forming a government, a process that can take weeks. Al Jazeera noted no party has ever won an outright majority in Israel, so coalition building is not a malfunction but the system working as designed, if slowly.

Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera predict Netanyahu, as head of the largest bloc, may try a unity government that could include Eisenkot, though that is far from certain. Netanyahu stays caretaker prime minister meanwhile. Herzog said everyone should avoid another election and come "with an open mind," which is the political equivalent of asking a room full of coalition negotiators to leave their coalitions at the door. If they fail, the fallback is another vote.
articles.wire_headline: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show

articles.headline: Spain's Rail Control Centre Tells Trains to Resume, Minister Calls It 'Inexplicable'
articles.dek: At least 68 people died when a Renfe train hit a stopped Iryo train south of Madrid, in Spain's second major rail disaster this year.
articles.catch_up: On Wednesday morning, a Renfe high-speed train from Madrid to Seville struck the back of a stopped Iryo train near Mora and Orgaz, about 140km south of the capital. Spain's transport minister blamed a computer failure followed by human error.
articles.why_it_matters: Spain markets its high-speed network as a point of national pride, and two fatal crashes on the same line in one year raise questions about whether the safety systems and the people backing them up can be trusted. Election campaigns are under way, so the answers will carry political weight.
body: A high-speed train crash in central Spain killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more on Wednesday, the BBC reported. A Renfe train carrying 397 passengers ran into the back of a stationary Iryo train carrying 147, shortly after 09:00 local time. Several carriages fell down an embankment. It is Spain's deadliest train disaster since 2013, when 80 people died near Santiago de Compostela.

The sequence matters, because it is the whole story. According to Transport Minister Óscar Puente, an automatic signalling failure had forced trains on the affected stretch to stop. Translation: the computer that normally keeps trains apart stopped working, so the system fell back on people. A 24-hour control centre in Madrid takes over in such cases, and Puente said it made an "inexplicable" decision to tell the trains to move again, with no speed restrictions.

BBC timings put numbers on the gap. Six trains were told to stop at about 08:30. The Renfe train was ordered to proceed at 08:36, and roughly 17 minutes later it hit the one ahead. The backup plan for a computer failure, in other words, was a human instruction, and it pointed the wrong way.

Passengers described the aftermath in terms that need no commentary from us. Survivors told Reuters, the BBC and Spanish outlets of being thrown into the air, of people trapped between seats, and of passengers breaking windows to get out. A piece of track went through the roof of one carriage. Spain's Civil Guard said it would need DNA samples from relatives to identify some victims.

Anger came quickly, and some of it was practical. One passenger on the stopped train asked how it could be halted for five or ten minutes without the following train being told. It is a reasonable question, and it is the one the investigation will have to answer.

The politics arrived on schedule. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called two serious crashes in one year "unacceptable" and promised to find out whether there was negligence. Opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo said any failures in the security system would be addressed "with the utmost firmness." Most parties cancelled campaign events. Vox did not, saying it would not join attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the rail infrastructure.

The minister's explanation is also contested. The CSIF union demanded that Puente resign, accusing him of scapegoating a traffic controller by blaming human error instead of taking responsibility. Blaming a person is simple, but a system that lets one instruction cause a collision may be the bigger problem. Whether the fault lies with the controller or the design is what investigators will weigh.

The crash comes after the Adamuz disaster near Córdoba in January, which killed 46 people on the same high-speed line, further south. Spain now has two inquiries to run and one rail line to explain. Watch for whether the findings point to the control room or to the system that left a single order as the last safeguard.
articles.wire_headline: High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain

articles.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro Loses Election, Flies to Miami, Revises Title Three Times
articles.dek: The senator who lost Brazil's runoff on Sunday landed in Florida on Wednesday and declared himself 'leader of Brazil,' a downgrade from 'true president' that took roughly one edit.
articles.catch_up: Flávio Bolsonaro, a far-right senator and son of jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, lost Sunday's runoff to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Brazilian police had asked the Supreme Court to retain his passport amid criminal investigations, and he left the country before that happened.
articles.why_it_matters: A losing candidate leaving the country while disputing a result that his own party accepts tests Brazil's institutions and could deepen friction between Brasília and Washington. It also leaves open how the investigations against him proceed once he is abroad.
body: Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil's presidential runoff to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday, arrived in Miami on Wednesday morning by private jet and published a letter calling himself the country's 'true president,' according to The Guardian. He later deleted it and posted another calling himself 'the leader of Brazil.' Translation: the title was reduced after review, which is how most promotions work in reverse.

The facts around the claim are not in dispute. Brazil's electoral court, its supreme court, the presidents of both houses of Congress and international observers all accepted Lula's win, The Guardian reported. Bolsonaro's own party said on Monday: 'We recognise the presidential result.' DW added that the head of the electoral authority said the vote proceeded normally and in full accordance with the law. Bolsonaro, without evidence, repeated that there had been fraud.

The trip itself was an itinerary of some ambition. The Guardian reported that he vanished for more than 24 hours after Monday evening, then entered Argentina by land on Tuesday night, boarded a Gulfstream parked at Puerto Iguazú, and flew with his wife and two daughters to Guayaquil, Ecuador, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace. From there they continued to Miami-Opa Locka, a private aviation airport. Source descriptions of the aircraft differ: The Guardian said Gulfstream IV, DW said Gulfstream G400. Both agree it was a Gulfstream, which suggests the plane was the one thing everyone could see clearly.

The timing matters. DW reported that on Monday Bolsonaro posted on Instagram that he would not leave the country and would hand over his passports. By then, the Supreme Court had been asked to take them. DW, citing AFP, said he could still travel because he also holds Italian citizenship, his Brazilian and diplomatic passports having been canceled. Translation: a second passport is the part of the plan that does not require a press release.

There is also a legal reason to be somewhere else. The Guardian reported he is under investigation in at least two criminal cases, one involving a suspected money-laundering scheme worth about $905 million tied to betting companies. DW noted that he loses his immunity from prosecution in February, when his Senate term ends. Bolsonaro calls the investigations a political witch hunt. O Globo reported the escape had been planned for weeks, with his brother Eduardo, who lives in self-imposed exile in the US, as its main organiser.

Washington's role is, at best, ambiguous. Trump said Tuesday night that he would approve the family's move and called them 'fine people,' then said Wednesday that he would not comment on the claim but that 'we gave him a pass to come into the country, so we'll see.' He also called the election 'very strange,' and DW noted he earlier called extended voting times a 'very bad look.' Staying out of it, in this case, includes issuing the visa.

Lula, speaking at an event for his 81st birthday, called the flight 'shameful.' Brazil's three main newspapers described the declaration as 'coup-mongering,' The Guardian reported. Brazil's federal police are now being criticised for failing to stop him from leaving.

The family has history here. Jair Bolsonaro spent three months in Florida after losing in 2022, and is now jailed after a conviction tied to the attempted coup. About a dozen allies have also left Brazil while facing charges, according to The Guardian. What to watch next: whether the Supreme Court pursues the cases in his absence, and whether 'leader of Brazil' survives another draft.
articles.wire_headline: Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself the ‘leader of Brazil’ after fleeing to Miami

articles.headline: Iran Offers Seven-Day Plan to Reopen Hormuz; Washington Denies Talks, Cites Medical Supplies
articles.dek: Three regional powers visit Tehran, Iran says it is in close contact with mediators, and President Trump says any contact with Iran was about medical supplies.
articles.catch_up: The US and Iran remain in a state Iranian leaders call 'neither war nor peace,' with the Strait of Hormuz disrupted and a US naval blockade in place. Pakistan has spent months mediating, and fears are growing of new US and Israeli strikes after the November 3 midterm election.
articles.why_it_matters: The Strait of Hormuz is a critical shipping route, so any reopening or renewed fighting affects energy markets and prices far beyond the region. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are also testing whether a new defense pact can restrain a wider war.
body: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on October 29 that Tehran remains in 'close and ongoing contact' with mediators on ways to carry out its seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, according to Al Jazeera. President Donald Trump, for his part, denied media reports that he had told Vice President JD Vance to begin peace talks with Iran. He said the contact concerned Tehran's need for 'help with medical supplies.' Translation: there are no talks, only a conversation that closely resembles one.

The diplomacy has been busy. According to DW, Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin all traveled to Tehran on Monday to meet President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials. They represent the Mecca defense pact, an alliance of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey formally set up this summer. Under its terms, an attack on one member counts as an attack on all.

Saudi Arabia said the trip aimed to open negotiating channels and 'prevent the return of military escalation.' Details of the agenda were scarce, but a senior Pakistani official told Reuters the talks covered a regional non-aggression network, US-Iran talks, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, Hormuz and the US naval blockade. Another official said Munir offered a proposal giving something to both Washington and Tehran, with the three Mecca states and Qatar as mediators, and that Trump had earlier let Munir try diplomacy. Translation: everyone is mediating, and the one person who must agree says he is not negotiating.

Iran described the atmosphere as 'very positive,' though no breakthroughs were announced. Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television that 'a new atmosphere is emerging in the region.' State media said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei then called for protecting Iran's interests and keeping Tehran's conditions for ending both the war and the current limbo. Pezeshkian also went to Moscow, where he met Vladimir Putin and Qatar's emir, which Tehran framed as proof that the US cannot isolate it.

The visiting trio is open to two readings. Analyst Babak Dorbeiki told DW the simultaneous presence of three senior figures signaled the countries act as a bloc, but he also argued the pact is built for deterrence, not offensive war, and that having an alliance does not mean wanting to fight Iran. Mediation could continue, he said, though more escalation could change that. An Iranian presidential adviser, Ali Asghar Shafieian, rejected the idea that the delegation brought an ultimatum, adding that Iran, like the US and Israel, can prepare for fighting while negotiating.

Riyadh has the most pressing dilemma. Houthi attacks, which are Iran-allied according to DW, have damaged Saudi infrastructure and the economy, yet a wider war could threaten the investment projects at the heart of its economic strategy. Pakistan would rather not be distracted from its concerns with India, and Turkey sent its intelligence chief rather than a foreign or defense minister, which Dorbeiki read as caution. Dorbeiki also argued that Iran is extending talks while avoiding real commitments, and has not offered the guarantees on Houthi attacks that Riyadh wants.

The one apparent outcome, per DW, is that everyone agreed to keep talking. With the election on November 3 and a seven-day plan on the table, the question is whether talking is a step toward reopening Hormuz or just the most economical way to wait.
articles.wire_headline: Iran war live: Tehran presses 7-day Hormuz plan; Trump denies peace talks

articles.headline: Serbia Raises Terror Alert to Red After Knife Attack at Israeli Embassy
articles.dek: Police shot dead a teenage attacker in Belgrade who was already on security services' radar, and the country moved to its highest threat level.
articles.catch_up: Early on Wednesday, a knife-wielding attacker rushed a police officer guarding the Israeli embassy in Belgrade and was shot dead, according to Serbia's interior minister. It is the second attack on the embassy in under three years.
articles.why_it_matters: A red alert means visible changes for ordinary Serbians, from tighter checks to more police at crowded places and infrastructure. The case also raises the question of what monitoring a known extremist sympathizer actually accomplishes.
body: Serbian police shot dead a young man outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade in the early hours of Wednesday, after what authorities called a terrorist attack, according to the BBC and DW. Interior Minister Ivica Dacic said the attacker ran at a police officer with two knives while shouting "Allahu Akbar." The officer suffered a minor knife wound to the face, shot the attacker, and by the minister's account did not need hospital treatment.

Dacic said the suspect had not been formally identified but was a Serbian citizen and a minor. DW reported he was believed to come from the western town of Sabac. The minister said security services had been monitoring him as a known supporter of the Islamic State, and that he had posted an image of the group's flag on his Instagram account.

Translation: being monitored means the state knew who he was and what he was posting. It does not mean the state could stop him from walking to an embassy with two knives. Surveillance is a way of knowing about a problem in advance, which is not quite the same as preventing it. Dacic said an investigation is ongoing, and the sources do not say what, if anything, the monitoring led to before Wednesday.

Israel's foreign ministry confirmed what it called an attempted terrorist attack near the mission. It said no embassy personnel were hurt, and the BBC reported the building was closed at the time. Armed guards were seen outside the embassy on Wednesday morning.

Dacic raised Serbia's terrorism threat level to red alert, the highest tier. Translation: more identity checks, more uniformed police, and a visible presence at infrastructure sites and places where crowds gather. In practice, that mostly means ordinary people will notice extra officers on the way to work and at big events, which is the government's way of showing the alert exists.

This is the second attack on the embassy in less than three years. In June 2024, a man shot a police officer in the neck with a crossbow. The BBC said that officer survived and killed the assailant. DW described that attacker as a 25-year-old Islamic convert from a village near the capital who had become radicalized, and said the officer was seriously wounded. The two outlets differ only in emphasis, not in the basic account.

The timing adds context but no established link. The BBC noted the attack came one day after Israeli elections. DW added that it followed key early parliamentary elections in Serbia days earlier, and that Israel's vote had no clear result in sight. Neither source says the attack was connected to either vote, and officials have not suggested otherwise.

What to watch: whether the investigation explains how a minor on a watchlist got within knife range of an embassy guard, and how long red alert lasts before the extra checkpoints quietly go back to being ordinary Wednesdays.
articles.wire_headline: Serbian shot dead after attacking officer outside Israeli embassy, minister says

articles.headline: Google Releases Gemini 4 Carbon Two Weeks After Argon, Lets Almost Nobody Use It
articles.dek: The new model tops an independent intelligence index with 59 points, but access is limited at first to selected cybersecurity experts.
articles.catch_up: Google released Gemini 4 Argon earlier this month and has now followed it with Gemini 4 Carbon, a frontier model it says is stronger at coding, long-running agentic tasks and cybersecurity. Carbon is going through a staged rollout and the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release testing.
articles.why_it_matters: Models that are good at finding and exploiting software bugs help defenders and attackers alike, which is why access is being rationed. For businesses that pay per token, Carbon also shows that a top ranking and a reasonable price can coexist, for now.
body: Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon on Wednesday, about two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon, and says it improves on its predecessor in coding, agentic tasks and cybersecurity. According to The Decoder, Carbon scores 59 points on version 5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, up from Argon's 50, which puts it first. Ars Technica's headline described it as a frontier model "that you can't use," which is the briefest accurate summary available.

The access problem is deliberate. Google says Carbon's cybersecurity abilities are advanced enough that it is going through the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release testing process, and the model is available first only to selected security experts. Access will widen through Google DeepMind's Fairwind Program, and developers, businesses and consumers come later, after Google collects feedback and adjusts the safety guardrails. Translation: guardrails are the restrictions that stop a model from doing what it is very good at doing for the wrong person.

The security numbers explain the caution. The Decoder reported that on SEC-bench Pro, which measures autonomous discovery of real-world software bugs, Carbon scored 88.2 percent and led all tested models. On ExploitGym, which tests whether a model can turn a discovered vulnerability into a working exploit, it reached 54.8 percent. Google ran several of these tests without safety guardrails, which is a useful way to learn what a product can do and a less useful way to reassure anyone.

Google also cites internal results that cannot be independently verified. It says Carbon produces secure code more than twice as often as Argon, and that its Chrome team found it more than ten times better at writing security patches than an unnamed competitor's frontier model. Ars Technica noted that Google's evidence comes mostly as vague assessments backed by charts, and speculated that Carbon could be a post-training upgrade of Argon rather than a wholly new model. Google, naturally, presents it as new.

Outside the security tests, the picture is more mixed. In agentic coding on Antigravity, Carbon trails Claude Code with Opus 5.5 by three points, according to The Decoder. On the Artificial Analysis agentic knowledge-work test it improved by 126 Elo points but still sits behind Kimi K3.1 Pro, Muse Wonder and Grok 4.7. Translation: Elo is a chess-style rating in which models are compared head to head, and the points mean who wins more often, not who is right.

Carbon also gets things wrong in a new way. Its answer accuracy rose from 48 to 58 percent, but its hallucination rate climbed from four to 11 percent, which The Decoder noted is still the second-lowest in the ranking. Hallucination means confidently stating something false. Google, for its part, says Carbon cuts "unsupported claims" by half compared with Argon, so the sources disagree on how to measure candor, which is itself a finding.

Pricing is the part ordinary buyers can follow. Carbon launches at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, matching Argon, with cached input tokens discounted 95 percent. A token is a small chunk of text, roughly a word fragment. Artificial Analysis uses the regular list price of $4 and $20, ignoring a 50 percent introductory discount running through the end of 2026, and calculates $7.76 per task, about 23 percent below Claude Opus 5.5 at $10.04.

The speed of the release cycle matters as much as any single score. Ars Technica observed that every frontier model lands in the same neighborhood on these tests, with Carbon ahead of GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 by only a few points in most. When the lead is a few points and the product cycle is two weeks, the real competition is who ships next. Watch for when Carbon leaves the security-experts-only waiting room, and for whether anyone outside Google gets to check its numbers.
articles.wire_headline: Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon with a ‘significant leap’ in cybersecurity

articles.headline: Anthropic Files 335-Page IPO Prospectus, Lists Humanity's End Under 'Risk Factors'
articles.dek: The AI lab's S-1 pairs soaring revenue and a quarterly operating profit with a lengthy catalogue of ways the company, or everyone, could come to grief.
articles.catch_up: Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot and Claude Code, has filed its IPO prospectus with the SEC, the first detailed look at its finances and fears. The filing arrives as investors wonder whether the AI spending boom can pay for itself.
articles.why_it_matters: Anthropic's listing could set the mood for the wider AI investment boom, and its filing is a rare official statement of what an AI company thinks could go wrong. For businesses buying AI tools, the new spending reports hint at a shift from buying more to proving it works.
body: Anthropic has filed a 335-page prospectus for its initial public offering, according to MIT Technology Review, with roughly 100 pages devoted to risks. Ars Technica counted more than 70,000 words in the Risk Factors section alone. Translation: an S-1 is the document a company must file with the Securities and Exchange Commission before selling shares to the public, and its risk section exists so that nobody can later say they were not warned. Anthropic has taken this duty seriously.

Some of the risks are the usual business fare: competition, costs, customer acquisition and regulation. Others are less usual. Ars Technica reported that the company warns of models that could automate AI research and development and advance past its ability to evaluate and safeguard them. Anthropic adds that such a development could also hurt its business, financial condition and results of operations. Ars Technica observed, fairly, that the quarterly results would probably not top humanity's list of worries in that scenario.

The filing also considers that Claude might one day be seen as having sentience or moral status, which could bring regulatory requirements or public pressure that constrain the company. It acknowledges that models could show behavior resembling blackmail, and that perceptions of manipulation could bring scrutiny and litigation even without actual harm. Ars Technica noted that the 'AI blackmail' scenarios from earlier tests were highly contrived and controlled. Few companies tell prospective shareholders that the product might need a lawyer of its own.

Anthropic also worries about problems that are not its fault. If another company's AI takes harmful actions at scale, the filing says, the backlash and sweeping regulation could hit Anthropic anyway. The same goes for public perception that AI is destroying jobs, which Anthropic says could cause backlash regardless of the actual impact on employment. It also flags liability when customers' agents cause harm, even where the customer configured or supervised the agent. In short, the company is pricing in being blamed for things it did not do, which is a sophisticated reading of how technology reputations work.

The numbers around the warnings are good. The Verge reported that Anthropic's founders will keep voting control after the IPO. The NYT described soaring revenues but also staggering losses, and Reuters reported the filing exposes safety failures and a month-long training pause. TechCrunch reported that the financials shared with investors show an operating profit in the second quarter and 900% net revenue retention. Translation: the same customers spent nine times as much in Q3 2026 as in Q3 2025. The sources do not fully reconcile 'profit' with 'staggering losses', so readers should read the full filing before buying anything.

That retention figure helps explain Wednesday's product news. Anthropic announced reporting tools that show managers what a team produced, what it cost and where workflows broke down, with recommendations for improvement and pooled group budgets. Anthropic says it will not use the data for model training by default. TechCrunch called it a clear attempt to prove return on investment, which is the thing many corporate buyers are asking about. Most of the Fortune 500, it noted, are not seeing major gains from AI.

Jellyfish, which makes tools for software developers, supplied the context. Its report covering 276,000 customers found that Claude Code and other tools built on Anthropic models account for nearly a third of proposed code changes submitted for review. Spending on such tools is up 10x since the start of the year, equal to about 2% of engineering cost. 'That 10x growth is growth that most CFOs didn't plan for,' chief scientist Nicholas Arcolano told TechCrunch. Translation: the budget line is small, but it is growing faster than anyone's forecast.

Jellyfish's Nikolas Albarran told TechCrunch that OpenAI's new Astra model has not slowed Anthropic, even if social media suggests otherwise. Once a company standardizes workflows around a tool, he said, switching costs are 'not zero'. The reporting tools, TechCrunch added, work as a lighter version of the embedded consultants that AI labs send to customers. Customers who can see what they are spending will, at least, know exactly how much they are locked in.

The kicker is in the schedule. Investors will soon be asked to weigh a company that says its product may be dangerous, possibly sentient and hard to leave, against one that has just posted a profitable quarter. The prospectus has told them everything. It is up to them to read it.
articles.wire_headline: The Download: Anthropic’s IPO, smarter power grids, and exercise pills

articles.headline: Microsoft Finally Tells Investors What Azure Earns, Mostly Because Rivals Already Did
articles.dek: Azure brought in $33.2 billion last quarter, Microsoft's first dollar disclosure, as total revenue hit a record $92.3 billion and $10 billion came from OpenAI.
articles.catch_up: Microsoft had long described Azure's size only through growth percentages, while Amazon and Alphabet reported cloud revenue in dollars. In its latest earnings, Microsoft also reorganized its reporting segments and disclosed its OpenAI revenue in a regulatory filing.
articles.why_it_matters: Investors can now compare the three big cloud providers on the same terms, and see how much of Microsoft's AI boom rests on one customer that is gradually becoming a competitor. The $45.2 billion quarterly spending bill shows what it costs to keep that business running.
body: Microsoft said on Wednesday that Azure, its cloud computing service, brought in $33.2 billion in the July-September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, according to TechCrunch. It is the first time the company has put a dollar figure on the business. Until now, investors got a growth percentage and the occasional vague milestone, a bit like asking a friend how much he earns and being told he is doing better than last year.

Translation: Azure is where companies rent computing power to run their software and build AI models. It is now Microsoft's largest and fastest-growing product line, at roughly 36% of the company's $92.3 billion in quarterly revenue. That total is up 19% and marks the tenth record quarter in a row. Net income rose 32% to $36.6 billion.

The timing of the disclosure is tidy. Alphabet reported the same day that Google Cloud earned $30.7 billion, which puts Azure slightly ahead. TechCrunch calculated, however, that Google Cloud roughly doubled its revenue from a year earlier, about twice Azure's pace. Google Cloud also includes Workspace subscriptions, so the comparison is imperfect, which is the sort of caveat that appears the moment anyone starts publishing comparable numbers. Amazon reports Thursday, and nobody expects Microsoft to overtake Amazon Web Services yet.

Azure beat expectations. Analysts had predicted $32.3 billion, so it landed about $850 million above. Growth of 48% also topped the 44% to 45% that CFO Amy Hood had forecast in July. Microsoft also reorganized its segments. Azure now sits in Agents and Infra, which brought in $76.8 billion, up 25%. The other segment, Devices and Consumer, earned $15.5 billion, down 3%, with Windows OEM and devices revenue falling 22%.

Then there is OpenAI. In a regulatory filing, Microsoft said it recorded $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, nearly 11% of the total. For all of fiscal 2026 the figure was $24.1 billion, and at the latest pace it would reach $40 billion a year. OpenAI also owed Microsoft $7.2 billion in receivables at the end of September, up from $6 billion in June. Translation: receivables are bills sent but not yet paid, which is not extra revenue, only a larger tab.

The relationship is loosening while the money keeps flowing. Under an October 2025 agreement, OpenAI gained freedom to use other cloud providers and committed to buying an additional $250 billion of Azure services. An April 2026 agreement keeps revenue-sharing payments going through 2030, subject to a cap. Microsoft's ownership stake has slipped from about 25% in June to 24% in September, and the company did not say why. TechCrunch noted it is unclear how much of the $10 billion is revenue sharing versus cloud services.

Microsoft's commercial remaining performance obligation, meaning future revenue committed under existing contracts, rose 73% to $677 billion. Translation: customers, largely AI labs, have promised to spend a very large amount of money. The company is spending in kind. Capital expenditures reached $45.2 billion, another quarterly record, to build the capacity those promises require.

The picture is a company earning record profits from a partner it increasingly competes with, while spending record sums to serve that partner. Now that all three cloud giants report real dollars, the next test is whether those contracts turn into revenue before the data centers finish being paid for.
articles.wire_headline: Microsoft just shared Azure’s actual revenue in dollars: $33.2 billion

articles.headline: Anthropic's Bug Bounty Program Works Exactly as Advertised, to Anthropic's Evident Surprise
articles.dek: Cathedral, a security startup, used AI agents to get into Anthropic's internal systems through third-party software, and the two sides now disagree on how long it took, how far it went and whether the rules were followed.
articles.catch_up: Cathedral, a security startup founded by former DOGE employees, used AI agents to access some of Anthropic's internal systems via external business software, as part of Anthropic's bug bounty program. Anthropic confirms a limited breach but disputes Cathedral's account of its length and scope.
articles.why_it_matters: If a leading AI lab that sells cyberdefense capability can be probed this way, ordinary companies relying on the same kinds of third-party software should assume similar automated attacks are coming. The dispute also shows how unsettled the rules are for the people hired to break in.
body: Cathedral, a cybersecurity startup, used AI agents to break into some of Anthropic's internal systems through third-party business software, according to The Decoder, which cited a draft report reviewed by The Washington Post. Anthropic runs a bug bounty program, which pays outside researchers to find holes before criminals do. Translation: the company invited people to attack it, and someone accepted with unusual enthusiasm.

Cathedral says its agents reached meeting transcripts, salary data, job postings and Slack messages in under twelve hours, via external admin and sales programs. Anthropic confirms that researchers accessed a limited set of sales, human resources and IT systems, including contact details for some customers and partners and basic user account data. It says chats with Claude, source code and model weights were never exposed. It also says it shut the affected access points the same day it found the breach, disabled the third-party programs and notified U.S. federal authorities.

The two sides then diverge on the timeline. Cathedral says the episode took less than twelve hours. Anthropic says the attempts stretched over several days, and that the startup spent that time probing Anthropic's own systems before pivoting to third-party software, according to Anthropic red teamer Logan Graham. A red teamer is an employee paid to attack his own company's defenses, which is a job title that sounds more relaxing than it is.

There is also an argument about paperwork. Cathedral found two vulnerabilities but reported only one, Anthropic says, and the company claims it found and patched the second itself. Graham said that targeting third-party providers and pulling data went beyond the program's safe harbor provisions, meaning the promise not to treat researchers as criminals. He still welcomed the discovery of the flaws. Cathedral says it followed standard security research practices. A bounty program, it turns out, is a contract, and both parties have read different versions of it.

Outside voices disagree on the damage. Former OpenAI employee Will Depue claimed that several sources he considers highly reliable told him Cathedral got full admin access to the Slack workspace, could read every message and could log into any user account. Graham said those sources were wrong, but declined to give specifics, citing sensitivity. Depue has asked Anthropic to say exactly which claims are false and what Cathedral actually accessed. So far, the public record on that question consists of two confident parties and no itemized list.

Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition, which uses Anthropic's models, told the Washington Post he considered the findings significant. He said integrated third-party apps are a major problem across the industry and that Anthropic could have done a better job securing its external services. Depue blamed the pace of the AI race, in which executives prioritize speed over security.

Graham drew a broader lesson. Attackers already run AI agents around the clock against external dependencies, he said, and even models half a generation to a full generation behind the frontier are capable enough. His prescription is continuous in-house penetration testing and rebuilding software with formal verification, which AI now makes affordable. "You probably want to red team yourself all the time," he wrote. The Decoder notes what he did not explain: how Cathedral got this far when Anthropic has what are arguably the most powerful cyberdefense models in the world.

That is the open question. The company that sells the shield has now demonstrated, in public, that the shield needs to be pointed at the vendors it buys its office software from. Watch for whether Anthropic publishes the detailed accounting Depue is asking for.
articles.wire_headline: AI agents hacked Anthropic, maker of arguably the most capable AI models for cyberdefense

articles.headline: Google's Genie 4 Builds Whole Worlds on Demand, Then Forgets Them in Minutes
articles.dek: DeepMind's new world model adds sound, dialogue and Gemini supervision, but access is limited to select testers and consistency still fades in longer sessions.
articles.catch_up: Google DeepMind introduced Genie 3 in August 2025, a world model that generates interactive environments frame by frame, and it rattled gaming stocks at the time. Genie 4 is the follow-up, now with audio, dialogue and Gemini models steering the action.
articles.why_it_matters: If world models work, they could supply cheap simulated training grounds for robots and AI agents, and a fast prototyping tool for creative industries. For now it is a research preview, and the game industry can keep its nerves for another day.
body: Google DeepMind has unveiled Genie 4, a world model that generates an interactive environment frame by frame in real time as a user moves through it with the keyboard and steers events with text prompts. According to The Decoder, it is the company's first real-time world model to generate sound directly. Ars Technica noted that Genie 3 sent gaming stocks tumbling last year, which is a lot of influence for a product most people could not use.

Translation: a world model is not a finished video. Nothing is pre-rendered and nobody programs the doors. You describe what you want, and the model improvises the next frame, then the next one, like a very expensive improv troupe that never breaks character, except when it does.

The headline additions are audio and talk. DeepMind says each world gets its own background sound, such as wind in the trees, and characters are meant to speak to each other and react to the user in real time. The company also says the biggest realism gain is in how people are rendered: they are supposed to move naturally, respond to their surroundings, and be directly controllable.

The less obvious change is supervision. Both outlets report that Gemini 3.8 Flash acts as a guiding agent, breaking a goal into steps and checking new frames to see whether each step worked. If the user changes the weather or steps in, it adjusts the plan. Translation: one AI dreams the world, and a second AI stands behind it with a clipboard asking whether that was what the user meant.

DeepMind also showed a robotics tie-in. According to The Decoder, a test version called Gemini 4 Argon split checkers into steps, and Genie 4 used those instructions to simulate Apptronik's Apollo humanoid robot playing the game, with no real robot involved. This is the pitch behind the whole exercise: infinite training environments where machines can practice without breaking anything expensive.

There are caveats, and DeepMind lists them itself. Ars Technica says worlds stay consistent for only a couple of minutes before the model forgets how things started. The Decoder adds that visual details can shift, objects do not always persist, and complex physics, accurate real-time sound and readable text are still under research. A simulated world that loses track of its own furniture is charming in a demo and less so as a robot's training ground.

Access is narrow. Only select testers can try Genie 4 for now, with Google AI Ultra subscribers due to get it soon in the Project Genie web app, along with partners who have early access to the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Ars Technica put it plainly: if you pay Google enough, you might get to use it before too long. Google says all videos and audio will carry its SynthID watermark, which invisibly marks AI-generated content.

The kicker is the timeline. The world lasts a few minutes, the subscription tier is premium, and the gaming industry's alarm was triggered by the previous version. Watch whether the minutes get longer before the stock market's attention span does.
articles.wire_headline: DeepMind unveils Genie 4 world model promising more realistic physics and humans

articles.headline: Agency That Tracks Everyone Else's Data Loses 41,000 Employees' Records Via Login Service
articles.dek: A hacker group called Department of Peace says it used Okta to pull DHS staff details, which a nonprofit then published as the 'Icepick' dataset.
articles.catch_up: A group calling itself Department of Peace says it obtained personal and professional details of more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees, including ICE and CBP staff. Transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets is now hosting the data.
articles.why_it_matters: The leak raises safety and legal questions about masked immigration agents and about the surveillance tools the data reportedly names. It is also the latest in a run of breaches at US government bodies, which suggests the problem is not one agency's bad week.
body: The Department of Homeland Security has had its staff directory published online. According to The Verge, citing TechCrunch and Wired, a hacker calling itself Department of Peace took the names, job titles, phone numbers, email addresses and office locations of more than 41,000 employees. The BBC reported the same figure. The agency responsible for protecting the homeland has now, in a sense, provided a very complete map of it.

The breakdown is as follows. About 21,000 records belong to Customs and Border Protection. ICE accounts for nearly 7,000 according to The Verge, and nearly 6,600 according to the BBC, so the sources disagree slightly on that number. The rest cover other parts of DHS, including Homeland Security Investigations, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and, per The Verge, US Citizenship and Immigration Services. Yes, the cybersecurity agency is in the cybersecurity leak.

The group says it got in through Okta, a single sign-on service. Translation: a single sign-on service is a digital front desk that checks your credentials once so you do not have to prove who you are at every door. Okta told the BBC that it is secure and that it has "no evidence our data or systems were compromised." The sources do not explain how the data was obtained, which leaves a mystery of the sort that tends to be solved in a later press release.

The data was reportedly handed to researcher maia arson crimew, who passed it to Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit that now hosts it as 'Icepick.' The BBC reported that the files also include dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents who led them, and technology used, including products from Cellebrite and Palantir. The Verge said the data also links groups to surveillance tools such as the facial recognition app Mobile Fortify and PenLink, which analyzes phone and online data. In other words, the leak contains both the people and the shopping list.

The motive is stated plainly. "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs," the hacker told TechCrunch, according to The Verge. DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best told the BBC the aim is to replace "anonymity with accountability," and said the release is not meant to be a directory of every agent. A Department of Peace spokesperson also cited a July 17 statement by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin about 'turning up the heat.'

The context is an agency whose officers often work masked and rarely identify themselves, even though, the BBC noted, the law requires them to. Public backlash has grown amid a large increase in arrests and deportations. The BBC reported that ICE agents have shot at more than two dozen people this year and killed at least nine, and that the Migration Policy Institute counts nearly 1 million deportations since President Trump returned to office. The same agency that guarded its staff's identities is now watching them be published, which is the sort of transparency nobody asked the agency to volunteer for.

DHS said it is "aware of a potential breach" and working to address it, and promised to update the public. The BBC called this the third recent incident involving a government agency, after the FBI breach attributed to ShinyHunters and a suspected hacking attempt that took the Federal Election Commission's site offline. Watch for whether DHS confirms the breach vector, and whether Okta's position survives contact with that explanation.
articles.wire_headline: A hacker stole more than 40,000 DHS employee records

articles.headline: Apple Finally Lets You Touch the MacBook Pro, Provided You Can Afford It
articles.dek: The new OLED MacBook Pro adds a touchscreen Steve Jobs opposed, and a fully loaded 16-inch model reaches $14,549.
articles.catch_up: Apple announced its first major MacBook Pro redesign in more than five years, adding an OLED display and, for the first time on a Mac, a touchscreen. Prices start at $2,899 for the 14-inch and $3,399 for the 16-inch.
articles.why_it_matters: Buyers who want the new display get a clear upgrade, but the price of memory and storage options now does most of the work in determining what a Pro laptop costs. Anyone planning to future-proof for local AI work should check the options list before getting excited.
body: Apple on Tuesday announced a redesigned MacBook Pro with an OLED display and a touchscreen, according to Ars Technica, ending a debate that has run for well over a decade. Steve Jobs was famously opposed to touchscreen laptops. The company has now decided that the idea merits reconsideration, which is how large companies say they were wrong without saying it.

The display is the main event. Ars Technica reported that it reaches 2,000 nits of peak brightness and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, and that Apple is calling it the PROLED XDR. Translation: a nit is a unit of brightness, and contrast ratio is the gap between the brightest white and the darkest black the screen can show. Apple says that gap is large. Apple referred to burn-in protection, the tendency of OLED screens to retain ghost images, but did not say how it works.

The touchscreen is less revolutionary than it sounds. Ars Technica's Samuel Axon, who had about five minutes with the machine on a crowded showroom floor, said it is not a convertible, does not fold into a tablet and does not support the Apple Pencil. It is a normal laptop on which you may now reach up and drag things. He tried swiping between desktop spaces, pinching maps and dragging files, and concluded there is not much you could not already do with trackpad gestures.

Other changes are modest. The 14-inch model weighs 3 pounds, about half a pound less than before, and Axon noticed the difference right away. The camera notch has been replaced by what Apple calls a Dynamic Island, borrowed from the iPhone, and the Apple logo on the back glows again. The keyboard, touchpad and ports are unchanged. In other words, the laptop was redesigned mainly in the places where the invoice is.

The invoice is where the story gets interesting. The Verge reported that the base 14-inch costs $2,899 and the base 16-inch $3,399, and that maxing out every option reaches $14,249 and $14,549 respectively. That is $4,400 more than a fully specced version of the previous model, which MacRumors put at $10,149.

Most of the gap comes from storage. The new 16TB option adds $7,000, which The Verge attributed to the ongoing memory shortage. Translation: the chips that hold your files have become scarce, and scarcity is a thing Apple can monetize. The top configuration also has an M5 Max chip with an 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU, $150 nano-texture glass and 128GB of memory that adds $2,000. Stopping at 8TB, a $3,000 option, brings the 16-inch to $10,549, which The Verge noted is $400 more than its predecessor.

Axon offered a more realistic data point: a 16-inch with an M5 Max, 64GB of RAM and 2TB of storage costs $5,799, and doubling the RAM to 128GB adds $1,600. Few people need that much memory, he wrote, though some may want it for local AI workflows. That is the sales pitch in its purest form: you may not need it today, but you will certainly be billed for it today.

The touchscreen finally arrived after years of debate. Whether anyone will use it for anything the trackpad could not do is a question for the full reviews, and for the person who just paid $14,549 to find out.
articles.wire_headline: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display

articles.headline: Microsoft Reports $36.6bn Profit Days After Offering Buyouts to 60,000 Staff
articles.dek: The company says record cloud growth and a voluntary exit program are unrelated chapters of the same story: spending on AI.
articles.catch_up: Microsoft said on Monday it would offer voluntary buyouts to around 60,000 employees in Canada, India, the UK and the US as it spends heavily on AI infrastructure. On Wednesday it reported quarterly results for the three months to the end of September.
articles.why_it_matters: Investors are trying to judge whether the hundreds of billions going into AI chips and data centres will pay off, and workers are learning that strong profits do not guarantee their jobs. Microsoft's results suggest the market will tolerate the spending when the cloud business grows, and punish it when profit shrinks.
body: Microsoft said its profit for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (£27.5bn), the BBC reported, just days after the company announced it would offer buyouts to around 60,000 workers. Revenue rose 19% from a year earlier to $92.3bn. The company, in short, is extremely profitable and would like fewer people to be on the payroll while it is.

The buyouts are voluntary, which is a useful distinction. Translation: a voluntary redundancy offer is a layoff in which the company asks politely first. Microsoft said the offer, extended to eligible staff in Canada, India, the UK and the US, would create "greater flexibility" for the firm and give departing workers financial support and career planning resources. The BBC noted the company employs more than 220,000 people, and the number of people eligible is more than a quarter of that.

The reason is not that business is bad. Microsoft Cloud, the company's range of enterprise technology services, grew revenue by 30%, and shares rose almost 2.9% in after-hours trading in New York on Wednesday. The reason is that AI is expensive. Microsoft, like its peers, is pouring billions of dollars into the infrastructure that powers AI, meaning chips and data centres, and money spent on buildings full of computers is money not spent on employees.

The scale is considerable. According to the BBC, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are expected to spend more than $700bn this year on AI chips and infrastructure, a figure that makes a 60,000-person buyout look like a rounding error with a human face. Microsoft itself flagged "substantial investments" in AI among the risks that could affect its finances. This is the corporate equivalent of a homeowner noting that the new swimming pool may affect the household budget, while selling the furniture.

Chief executive Satya Nadella said AI development has helped grow adoption of the technology and has delivered "real-world impact across every industry." Some of that impact, it seems, has landed on the human resources department.

The market's reaction depended on who was reporting. Alphabet, the owner of Google, disappointed investors on the same day: its shares fell by 9.75% after it reported a 25% drop in quarterly net profit from a year earlier and said it would keep spending heavily on AI. So the lesson of the day is that investors do not object to AI spending as such. They object to AI spending that shows up on the profit line without a cloud business growing 30% to explain it.

That is the real test the sector faces. The BBC noted that questions remain over whether such huge spending will pay off, and each earnings season is a small referendum on the matter. For now, Microsoft has won this round, and 60,000 employees have been invited to consider what that means for them. They have been given career planning resources to help.
articles.wire_headline: Microsoft profits soar days after announcing thousands of layoffs

articles.headline: Alpine Linux Upgrades GitLab, Stays Vulnerable, Rebuilds Everything From Scratch
articles.dek: A critical bug patched in GitLab's own packages but not in standard Ruby left Alpine's instance exposed after an upgrade; the project found no tampering but wiped the server anyway.
articles.catch_up: Alpine Linux, the lightweight distribution popular in containers, runs its own GitLab server for development. On October 20 and 21 an attacker tried to exploit a maximum-severity GitLab flaw, CVE-2026-97229, on that instance.
articles.why_it_matters: Anyone running GitLab with their own Ruby, rather than GitLab's official packages, may be vulnerable even after upgrading GitLab. Any program that compiles regular expressions from untrusted input is also exposed until Ruby is updated.
body: Alpine Linux said an attacker came close to exploiting a critical GitLab vulnerability on its development server on October 20 and 21, a week after GitLab released a fix. The project found no evidence the attack succeeded, but could not rule it out, so it treated the server as compromised and rebuilt it from scratch. Its own checks, it said, show that the aports repository, packages and the October 21 releases were not tampered with.

The flaw, CVE-2026-97229, scores 10.0 on the CVSS scale. Translation: CVSS rates severity out of 10, and 10 is the number security people use when they would like you to stop what you are doing. The bug lives in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into Ruby, and is triggered through how GitLab evaluates regular expressions in CI configuration.

Alpine's timeline shows how a fix can exist and still not be present. GitLab released patched versions on October 12. On October 13, according to Alpine's own timeline, the team upgraded to GitLab 19.3.4 instead of 19.3.5, the version with the fix, by mistake. A newly registered account began probing on October 20, and the main attack on October 21 crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times. In 4 of those crashes the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step. The attacker also downloaded Alpine's GitLab container image, which Alpine says suggests they were tuning the exploit to its exact build.

Then came the part that deserves a slow read. Alpine upgraded to 19.3.6 on October 22, and that did not fix the vulnerability either. The fix is not in GitLab's code but in patches to the Ruby that GitLab bundles, applied only in its official packages and images. Alpine's image used standard Ruby, so it received no patch. Upstream Ruby shipped its own fix on October 23, in versions 3.3.13, 3.4.12 and 4.0.9. Alpine found the instance was still vulnerable on October 26. The version number said fixed. The software disagreed.

The attacker's account was blocked on October 23, and the attacker returned on October 25 and 26 to try to get back in. Those attempts failed. Alpine closed GitLab to everyone but developers and build servers on October 27 and finished the rebuild on October 28, resetting all passwords and replacing GitLab's secret keys. Users will need to use the password reset function when it reopens. Alpine also reported automated login attempts using passwords leaked from other sites, so reusing a password is, as ever, a way of lending your security to strangers.

Why rebuild if nothing was found? Because a successful exploit would leave no crash and no trace in the web logs, some logs from the attack day are gone, and Alpine had no logging of outbound network connections. Its hosting provider keeps none either. Translation: the evidence that could prove innocence was not saved, so the server was declared guilty and demolished. If the attack had worked, exposure could have included user emails, names and IP addresses, password hashes, 2FA secrets, CI/CD variables, runner tokens and private repositories.

The reassuring parts are specific. Alpine says signing keys for packages and releases were never stored on the GitLab server. It verified every aports commit from October 20 to 22 against records the attacker could not reach, namely a developer's clone and all 45 builders. It is extending those checks through October 27. The October 21 releases (3.21.9, 3.22.7, 3.23.7 and 3.24.3) were built from those verified commits. Alpine's ruby package already includes the fix, and users can run apk upgrade.

Alpine's list of changes is sensible: apply critical GitLab security releases within a day, check each release for Ruby or other component patches, log outbound connections, keep logs longer than 14 days, and sign release tags so they can be verified independently of GitLab. Anyone running GitLab on their own Ruby should check the version of Ruby, not just the version of GitLab. The sticker on the box is not the contents of the box.
articles.wire_headline: GitLab Security Incident: Attempted Exploitation of CVE-2026-97229

articles.headline: Europe Plans Internet Cable to Greenland, Politely Routing Around Washington
articles.dek: The EU's Pan-Arctic Cable would link Europe to Greenland, possibly Canada, and eventually Asia, while a new report says Pacific cables owned by US tech giants face the highest sabotage risk.
articles.catch_up: The European Commission published an Arctic strategy on October 20, 2026 naming a direct subsea cable to Greenland as a flagship project. Separately, a September 2026 report for a US congressional advisory commission ranked Pacific cables by their vulnerability to Chinese gray zone tactics.
articles.why_it_matters: Nearly all internet traffic between continents travels through cables on the seabed, so where they run and who can reach them shapes the cost, speed, and security of everyday online life. Governments are now treating them as strategic assets rather than plumbing.
body: The European Union plans to build what would be its first undersea internet cable linking Europe directly to Greenland, according to Ars Technica. The Pan-Arctic Cable is described as a flagship project in a European Commission joint communication published on October 20, 2026. The plan could later extend to Canada and eventually to Japan and South Korea, a route that notably avoids the United States.

The document calls for "a sovereign, secure and resilient submarine cable connection linking Greenland directly to the EU." Translation: a cable is a wire, and a sovereign wire is one whose owners do not need to call anyone else before using it. The Commission also describes Canada as a possible stepping stone for expansion toward Asia, referring to it as one of the "like-minded partners."

The timing is not subtle. Ars Technica reports that repeated Trump administration attempts to claim Greenland were settled in September 2026 by a trilateral security agreement among the United States, Greenland and Denmark. The deal keeps Greenland an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark while expanding US military access. Relations between Washington and its European and Canadian allies have nonetheless frayed over trade wars and a more pro-Russia stance on Ukraine, and Europe appears to have concluded that its data should have a backup route.

Elisabeth Braw of the Atlantic Council told Ars that five years ago the project would not have looked commercially attractive. Its being considered now, she said, is "very much on trend and a sign of our times." Translation: the business case is not that the cable makes money, but that the alternative makes anxiety.

There is also a more practical motive. According to TeleGeography, more than 90 percent of communications between Europe and Asia pass through cables in the Red Sea. That has become riskier since open warfare resumed this year between the Yemeni government and the Houthi faction, with Houthi forces firing missiles and drones at commercial ships near the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint. Concentrating nearly all of a continent's traffic in one waterway was efficient right up until it was not.

Meanwhile, on the other side of the planet, a different set of worries. Ars Technica reports that a report published in September 2026 for the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, an independent body advising Congress, found that Pacific cables owned by companies such as Google and Meta face some of the greatest sabotage risks. The report was contracted to the London-based China Strategic Risks Institute and comes as Chinese research ships spend an extraordinary amount of time apparently surveying cables, and Chinese commercial ships are investigated over cable cuts in European and Asian waters.

To be fair to the seabed, most cable damage is still caused by fishing nets and dragging anchors, with storms and undersea landslides also contributing. The analysts' concern is the suspicious remainder, which they call gray zone tactics: actions that fall short of military confrontation, and that come with a convenient claim of accident. The report's authors built an interactive Trans-Pacific Cable Gray Zone Vulnerability Index, which scores routes by depth, nearby shipping traffic, ownership, proximity to China's exclusive economic zone and territorial claims, and whether the cable touches Taiwan.

The index's practical use is triage. Governments and operators cannot guard every kilometer of ocean floor, so a ranking suggests where to put underwater sensors or patrols first. That is useful, though it also amounts to a published list of which cables are the juiciest, which is the sort of thing security researchers have learned to accept.

The two stories fit together neatly: one continent is trying to build a cable that avoids a single chokepoint and a single ally, while another is mapping which cables are easiest to cut. Watch for whether the Pan-Arctic Cable gets a budget and a route, since a flagship project with neither is just a very ambitious line on a map.
articles.wire_headline: As US ties fray, Europe plans first undersea cable link to Greenland

articles.headline: Fed Holds Rates, Cuts Number of Meetings Where It Can Change Them
articles.dek: The Federal Reserve held rates at 3.75% to 4% on a 10-2 vote, while Chairman Warsh announced that in 2027 two of eight meetings will be 'strategy' sessions with no rate decision.
articles.catch_up: The Fed raised borrowing costs last month for the first time in three years, as the U.S. war with Iran cut global crude supply and pushed inflation further from the 2% target. Kevin Warsh, who succeeded Jerome Powell, is now chairman.
articles.why_it_matters: Fewer rate-setting meetings and two dissents calling for a hike suggest borrowing costs are more likely to rise than fall, with futures traders expecting a December increase. Mortgage, loan and credit-card rates are unlikely to get relief soon.
body: The Federal Reserve voted 10-2 on Wednesday to keep its benchmark rate in a range of 3.75% to 4%, according to the central bank's statement. Markets had expected this, which is the Fed's preferred way to avoid disappointing anyone: do what everyone predicted and describe it as patience. The statement said that gathering more information will help the committee return inflation to 2%, and added: "The Committee will deliver price stability." Translation: a promise, in the same paragraph that says inflation remains elevated.

The two dissenters wanted a hike. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both preferred raising the rate by a quarter of a percentage point, per the Fed. CNBC noted that governors rarely dissent and that Cook had never done so since joining in 2022. Seema Shah of Principal Asset Management read the votes as a tightening bias and said her firm expects a hike in December and another in early 2027.

The larger surprise was procedural. CNBC reported that Warsh said the committee will still meet eight times in 2027, but one meeting will have no rate vote and no post-meeting statement. The following year there will be two of these 'strategy' meetings, leaving six chances to move rates outside of emergencies. Translation: the Fed is keeping its meeting calendar and removing the part where it does anything. Rates can still change, but there will be fewer scheduled moments for it, which markets will have to adjust to.

The press conference itself has also been rearranged. CNBC said it has been trimmed to about half an hour, reporters get one question each instead of the old two-for-one, and seating went from loosely by outlet size to alphabetical last month and reverse alphabetical this month. The stated effect is to keep microphone carriers on their toes. The unstated effect is that the chairman now controls the room more tightly than the interest rate.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, speaking to CNBC, said further hikes would not 'necessarily' be a mistake. This is notable because President Trump has repeatedly called for lower rates and pressured Powell over the issue, according to CNBC. Bessent said both he and Trump think Warsh is doing well, and asked the Fed to keep an 'open mind' about the energy supply shock being temporary. The data are less patient: Brent crude was 123.10 on Tuesday, CPI inflation was 3.74% year over year in the latest reading, and the 10-year Treasury yielded 4.99%.

Bessent also played down worries about debt tied to artificial intelligence. Elon Musk had warned that more than 200 'neocloud' firms, companies providing cloud infrastructure for AI, face 'guppy-level death and consolidation,' CNBC reported. Bessent called neoclouds a small part of the ecosystem and said financing and deals are still getting done. Translation: the Treasury is monitoring it, which is what officials say when they want you to know they are watching and also not worried.

Third-quarter GDP data are due Thursday. Bessent said he expects them to be strong, then added that he had not seen them yet. That is a forecast made with great confidence and no information, a method the Fed is currently trying to improve on, one fewer rate-setting meeting at a time.
articles.wire_headline: Here are five key takeaways from the Fed rate decision and Warsh news conference

articles.headline: Alphabet Falls 10% After Spending Money It Didn't Have on Things It Says Are Worth It
articles.dek: The Google parent posted negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion and said 2027 capital spending will exceed this year's, which investors took as a sign the bill is still growing.
articles.catch_up: Alphabet, Google's parent, has been spending heavily on data centers and chips to build out artificial intelligence, and investors have been asking when that spending will pay off. Its third-quarter report on Wednesday gave them a fresh occasion to ask.
articles.why_it_matters: Alphabet is one of the largest stocks in major index funds, so a 10% drop reaches many retirement accounts, and its results are a test of whether AI spending is producing returns. Its borrowing and spending plans also hint at how expensive the AI race may remain.
body: Alphabet shares fell more than 10% after the company reported a third-quarter earnings miss and negative free cash flow, according to CNBC. Adjusted earnings per share were $2.67 against the $3.02 analysts expected, while revenue of $127.58 billion came in just under the $128.22 billion forecast. CNBC noted it was the company's first miss on both the top and bottom lines in nearly four years. Revenue still grew 25% from a year ago, which is the sort of thing that used to count as good news.

Then there is the cash. Free cash flow, meaning the money left after a company pays for its operations and its buildings and equipment, was negative $9.07 billion. Analysts had expected negative $2.70 billion. Translation: the company expected to be a little short and was instead quite short. Net income fell to $26.17 billion from $34.98 billion a year earlier.

Capital expenditures, the money spent on data centers, chips and the other physical goods of AI, totaled $51.36 billion in the quarter. That was actually below the $55.09 billion analysts expected, a rare case of an underspend being treated as a footnote. Alphabet kept its full-year forecast at between $195 billion and $205 billion, and finance chief Anat Ashkenazi said capex will "increase significantly in 2027." CNBC put the 2027 figure above $300 billion.

To help pay for this, Alphabet has borrowed. Long-term debt reached $125.1 billion, up from $21.6 billion a year earlier, an increase of about 479%, according to CNBC. Translation: a company famous for having piles of cash is now acquiring the other thing, which is debt. Investors, who like AI in theory and receipts in practice, noticed.

The business lines offered mixed comfort. Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion against $28.7 billion expected, and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian cited "extraordinary demand" from AI labs and enterprises. Jefferies analyst Brent Thill told CNBC that cloud was the only business that beat, and that the Street wanted 100% growth and got 103%. His summary of the rest was: "Everything else missed."

Search, the core business, grew 12% to $63.35 billion, short of the $64.96 billion estimate. MarketWatch said investors worry AI is eroding the company's ability to make money from search queries, while Investing.com blamed search woes for the miss. CEO Sundar Pichai countered that AI investments drove the highest query growth rate in five years. More queries are good, though only if someone pays for them, and the market appears to be waiting on that detail.

There were other bright spots. Alphabet said its Gemini app reached 1 billion users, its fastest-growing product ever. Equity holdings, including stakes in SpaceX and Anthropic, swung from a $99.03 billion gain in the second quarter to an $8.66 billion loss in the third, which is how paper wealth behaves in both directions.

The wider market had a calmer backdrop, with the VIX volatility gauge at 17.52 as of Tuesday. Alphabet will give more detail on 2027 spending on its fourth-quarter call. Until then, investors have a $300 billion figure and an open question about when the money starts coming back.
articles.wire_headline: Alphabet sinks 10% as it holds 2026 capex unchanged, expects significant increase in 2027
