articles.headline: Oracle Promises $225 Billion in Revenue, Stock Jumps 11% on Strength of Spreadsheet
articles.dek: The company's investor-day targets and a $20 billion cap on new fundraising calmed nervous creditors, at least until the money actually has to arrive.
articles.catch_up: Oracle spent the past year borrowing heavily to build AI data center capacity, including for OpenAI, and its shares had lost about a third of their value this year as investors worried about the bill. On Wednesday it held an investor day to explain how it intends to pay for all of it.
articles.why_it_matters: Oracle's debt load has become a gauge of how nervous markets are about paying for the AI buildout, and its credit rating sits one notch above junk. If the company's targets slip, the cost of borrowing for AI infrastructure could rise for everyone else too.
body: Oracle shares rose 11% on Wednesday after the company told investors it expects $225 billion in revenue in fiscal 2030 and will limit additional fundraising over that stretch to $20 billion, CNBC reported. The forecast implies average annual growth of 35%. The market, which had spent months asking whether Oracle could afford its ambitions, responded to a slide deck that said yes.

The financing plan covers fiscal 2027 through 2030, and Oracle said the $20 billion will be split equally between equity and debt. Translation: equity means selling new shares, which dilutes existing owners, and debt means borrowing, which Oracle has already done rather a lot. Half and half is the corporate version of splitting the check.

The reason for the nerves is on the balance sheet. According to CNBC, Oracle has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and holds a BBB- credit rating from S&P, the lowest level of investment grade above junk. Translation: it is one downgrade away from being classed with borrowers who pay the most to borrow. Its shares had fallen about a third this year on fears that rising interest rates would make the buildout too expensive.

The spending is not modest. FactSet figures cited by CNBC show capital expenditures more than doubled to $55.7 billion in fiscal 2026 and are expected to rise another 65% to $91.9 billion this year. Analysts expect negative free cash flow of about $35 billion this year and a similar amount next year. Translation: Oracle is spending far more than it earns, and will for a while.

Oracle's answer was a timeline. It said it will turn free cash flow positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 and reach more than $30 billion the following year, with operating margin topping 40% in fiscal 2030. It also said vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments should reduce upfront cash needs. In plain terms, suppliers will wait to be paid and customers will pay early, which is a clever way to have other people's money do the building.

The forecast was less of a shock than the stock move suggests. Analysts polled by LSEG already projected fiscal 2030 revenue of $224.2 billion, slightly below Oracle's own $225 billion. The news was less the number than the confidence that the company would not need to raise much more money to get there.

Credit markets were calmer but not convinced. The spread on Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, stood at 277 basis points after touching about 320 earlier this month, and is still up almost 100% this year. Translation: insuring $10 million of Oracle debt costs roughly $277,000 a year, down from about $320,000 a few weeks ago, and nearly double the start of the year.

The backdrop is not helpful. The 10-year Treasury yield stands at 4.99% and the 2-year at 4.7%, so borrowing remains expensive for everyone, including companies promising 35% growth. Oracle has now told investors when the cash will turn positive. The next step is doing it, which tends to be harder than presenting it.
articles.wire_headline: Oracle stock pops 11% as long-term revenue forecast and clarity on financing ease debt concerns

articles.headline: DoorDash Poised to Buy Instacart, Consolidating Humanity's Ability to Outsource Groceries
articles.dek: CNBC's sources say a roughly $17 billion deal could be announced Thursday, giving DoorDash a bigger grocery footprint and regulators something to read.
articles.catch_up: The Information reported last week that Instacart was exploring a sale and had talked with Uber and DoorDash. By Monday, several outlets said DoorDash was in advanced talks at a valuation of about $17 billion.
articles.why_it_matters: If the deal closes, two of the biggest names in app-based delivery would become one, which could affect fees, grocer bargaining power and prices for anyone who pays someone else to carry their milk. Antitrust reviewers will decide how much of that happens.
body: DoorDash's bid to buy Instacart could be announced as soon as Thursday morning, according to sources who spoke to CNBC. Instacart shares rose about 4% in extended trading on Wednesday, while DoorDash fell less than 1%. Translation: investors think the seller is getting a good price and the buyer is merely getting a lot of lettuce.

The reported price is about $17 billion, a figure several outlets attached to the talks on Monday. Neither company has confirmed it. Instacart declined to comment, and DoorDash had not responded to CNBC at the time of publication, which is the traditional way of saying a deal is real but not yet legally discussable.

The logic is straightforward. DoorDash began in restaurant delivery and has spent years adding retailers, including Sephora, Macy's, Staples and Anthropologie, plus a growing list of regional grocers after a partnership with Kroger last year. Instacart is the company that already does the grocery part at scale. Buying it is faster than building it, and considerably faster than asking customers to stop wanting avocados.

Instacart's side of the story is less sunny. It went public in 2023 after riding the pandemic surge in grocery delivery, but CNBC reports it has struggled to hold that momentum. In December it agreed to pay $60 million to settle Federal Trade Commission allegations that it misled users with false advertising and used what the agency called unlawful subscription enrollment practices. Translation: the FTC said some customers signed up for things more easily than they could understand them.

Then there is the competition. Amazon, after slowing its brick-and-mortar grocery effort, has pushed harder into online groceries and uses its fulfillment network for faster delivery. Walmart has also moved into same- and next-day service. Both threaten Instacart's model of having a person shop for you within the hour, which is convenient but expensive to staff. A sale to a larger partner looks less like a victory lap and more like a lifeboat with a very good valuation.

The remaining question is regulators. Analysts have said the combination could draw antitrust scrutiny, given overlapping markets. Wedbush analysts wrote that third-party delivery platforms remain a minority of total grocery consumption, but that viewing the market more narrowly, or from the grocers' perspective as enterprise customers, can make approvals more challenging. Translation: the merging companies will say they compete with Walmart and Amazon, and the regulators may ask whether that is the right comparison.

Markets, for what it is worth, are not panicking over any of it. The S&P 500 tracker SPY stood at 772.31 on Wednesday, and the VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, was 17.52 on Tuesday. Brent crude at $123.10 has apparently already supplied the week's anxiety quota, and consumers paying for delivery fees may notice the cost of getting groceries is not the only thing rising.
Watch Thursday morning for an announcement and then the long wait for review. The deal will be judged on whether groceries are a delivery market or just a very large market with deliveries in it.
articles.wire_headline: DoorDash's deal to buy Instacart coming as early as Thursday morning, sources tell CNBC

articles.headline: Britain Taxes Banks, Cuts Bills and Promises Markets It Will Not Frighten Them
articles.dek: Chancellor John Healey's first budget raises the bank surcharge to 6% for 15 months, scraps gas standing charges and keeps the fiscal rules intact, and gilt yields dipped.
articles.catch_up: Britain's new finance minister, John Healey, delivered his first budget as inflation hit 3.5% in September and borrowing costs climbed, with CNBC citing the U.S.-Iran war as a driver of fuel prices. Markets expect the Bank of England to raise interest rates next month.
articles.why_it_matters: Households get lower energy costs and one-off payments, while the government is betting that a temporary bank tax will pay for them without spooking bond investors. If the bet fails, the cost shows up in mortgage rates and public services.
body: John Healey, the U.K.'s finance minister, delivered his first budget on Wednesday, according to CNBC. It contained dozens of measures to ease living costs, a tax rise on banks, more money for defense and AI, and a promise that the government's borrowing rules remain in force. Markets reacted broadly positively, which in budget terms is the equivalent of a standing ovation from a very nervous audience.

The cost-of-living section is the part most voters will notice. Healey removed standing charges on household gas heating bills (Translation: the fixed daily fee you pay for being connected, regardless of how much gas you use), extended a tax break on electricity through July 2027, and promised £100 checks for households in the four lowest local housing tax bands, at a cost of £2.6 billion. Tariffs come off more than 100 grocery products, the minimum wage rises 3.9%, and a planned cut to tax-free savings thresholds was canceled.

The reason all this is necessary is that Britain imports a lot of its energy and so catches every external price shock. Annual inflation reached 3.5% in September, and Healey blamed the inflationary impact of the U.S.-Iran war, a conflict he said Britain did not want. It is an unusually direct budget argument: the chancellor is compensating citizens for a war they were not consulted on.

Someone has to pay, and Healey chose banks, gambling firms and vape shops. The bank surcharge rises by 3 percentage points to 6%, starting in January and ending 15 months later. Healey had called British banks the economy's "jewel" earlier this month, and then asked the jewel to fund the "breathing space" for households. This is the fiscal equivalent of complimenting someone's wallet before borrowing it.

The banks took it well. Barclays rose 3.3%, Lloyds more than 2.6% and NatWest 2.5%, because the increase was smaller than some in the sector had feared. Shareholders, it turns out, will cheer a tax rise provided it is the smaller of the two they were braced for. JPMorgan Chase was less cheerful, saying that singling out the industry again "lacks principle." CEO Jamie Dimon had earlier suggested the bank might rethink its Canary Wharf headquarters buildout if the government were hostile; on Wednesday the company said it remains "committed" to the U.K.

The bond market is the audience that matters most. Healey said his plans meet the fiscal rules, meaning day-to-day spending is covered by taxes rather than borrowing and debt falls as a share of GDP. The Office for Budget Responsibility, the official forecaster, estimated £15 billion of headroom by 2029/30 (Translation: a cushion between the plan and the rules, which a chancellor can lose with one bad forecast). It expects debt to reach 83.8% of GDP next year and fall to 81.7% by 2032, and it raised growth forecasts to 1.2% this year, 1% in 2027 and 1.6% in 2028. The 10-year gilt yield slipped 2 basis points (0.02 percentage points) to 5.323%.

Elsewhere there was something for most constituencies. The budget includes £10 billion in economic and military support for Ukraine, a path to NATO's 3.5% of GDP defense target by 2035 with 3% by 2030, hundreds of millions for AI security and sovereignty, and a data center "covenant" trading grid connections for local jobs and water protection. Founders get a reduced capital gains tax rate on gains up to £10 million. Healey also pledged to cut the welfare bill, which reached 10.7% of GDP in 2024/25, while saying he would not let disabled people suffer in a failing system. His predecessor Rachel Reeves watered down similar plans after a rebellion in her own party, so that promise has some history to live down.

The kicker is the calendar. The bank tax lasts 15 months, the Bank of England may raise rates next month, and the war driving the energy bills has no announced end date. The budget balances on the assumption that all three behave.
articles.wire_headline: The UK cuts energy bills, taxes banks and boosts defense in high-stakes budget
